title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality + fuzzy 5‑gram overlap + provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success rates. All execution artifacts are archived. The executed run used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json. Because no high‑confidence contamination flags were raised, the guarded policy performed no exclusions or replacements. Every baseline and guarded episode passed the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (baseline = 150/150; guarded = 150/150); paired difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0,0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We explicitly reclassify the prespecified primary confirmatory test as degenerate/uninformative for detecting web‑sourced contamination under the executed shared‑generation, synthetic‑sample regime, reconcile preregistration→execution using archived artifacts, document an implementation detail that suppressed global per‑item overlap persistence (execution/transformation_manifest.json), and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations (provenance‑rich public sampling, independent generation per condition, full per‑item overlap logging, multi‑model replication, paraphrase detectors) to make future contamination audits sensitive to realistic leakage modes.

sections.introduction:
Motivation and scope. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated and deployed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Reliable operational claims require that benchmark measurements reflect model capability rather than dataset contamination or templated leakage. Recent surveys and benchmark analyses call for contamination‑aware evaluation practices: deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance tracing, and validator‑backed oracles. This study preregistered a focused audit to test conservative contamination detectors and a guarded exclusion policy in a reproduceable pipeline and to verify whether applying those controls materially changes validator‑measured success rates.

Research question and bounded contribution. Our preregistered research question asked: under conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change a single hosted LLM's validator pass rate? We do not claim to measure contamination prevalence in independent public benchmarks here—rather, we report a fully preregistered, archived execution and an artifact‑grounded reconciliation explaining why the executed configuration produced a degenerate paired test. All reported numerical results (pairs = 150, baseline/guarded successes, contingency counts, bootstrap CI, and p‑value) are taken directly from archived analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work: Prior findings and gaps. System and benchmark papers show LLMs can translate intent into device configurations and propose repairs; tool‑assisted generate–validate pipelines and iterative repair loops improve average repair outcomes versus naive generation. Formal network verification techniques (Header Space Analysis and related localized subspecification methods) serve as practical oracles for reachability and policy checks and are commonly integrated into NetOps validation pipelines. Survey and meta‑evaluation work highlights two persistent risks in LLM evaluation: (1) contamination—benchmark items or templated phrasing appearing in model training data can inflate apparent accuracy—and (2) construct invalidity—benchmarks dominated by low‑complexity templates may not reflect operational difficulty. Our audit implements a conservative subset of recommended defenses and emphasizes a preregistration→execution reconciliation to show how execution choices affect audit sensitivity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen estimand. We preregistered the study as contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 and froze the primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration specified detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity brackets at 0.65/0.50), a guarded exclusion policy (exclude only high‑confidence flags), deterministic replacement rules with fixed seeds and intent‑similarity checks (cosine ≥ 0.85), and the analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar two‑sided test plus paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Planned confirmatory accounting was 150 items × 2 conditions = 300 episodes and a model call budget up to 300.

Sampling, generator semantics, and a crucial execution choice. The preregistration permitted deterministic synthetic generation for reproducibility but also listed public benchmark datasets as candidate sampling sources. The preregistered benchmark_scope named four public datasets (OpenAlex IDs in the preregistration). In the executed run the confirmatory sample was produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each generated item carries a source_identifier with prefix "synthetic-netops:" as recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (see archived manifest). Critically, execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Under shared_initial_candidate the pipeline issues a single hosted model generation per item and reuses that candidate for both baseline and guarded episodes unless a high‑confidence exclusion triggers replacement. This choice reduced provider calls (model_calls_used = 150) and mechanically collapses baseline vs guarded discordance when no exclusions occur; the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts record these counts and semantics.

Contamination detectors and persistence policy. The detector suite implemented the preregistered heuristics: normalized exact equality; fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with the preregistered thresholds; and provenance timestamp heuristics. Implementation detail (recorded in execution/transformation_manifest.json): to limit stored artifact volume, the detector workflow persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap tables only when a threshold crossing or replacement occurred. Consequently, when no items met the high‑confidence exclusion threshold the archive contains no global per‑item overlap table—this behavior is an explicit, documented implementation choice and explains the absence of a full overlap distribution in analysis artifacts.

Validator and scoring rule. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) enforces the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule: the parsed configuration must achieve the task's expected_final_state on allowed fields and respect workflow/transient constraints (sequence and protected interfaces). The validator outputs binary pass/fail and detailed traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, normalized_configuration) archived per episode and used for the confirmatory analysis (execution/scoring/*.json).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and contingency. The archived execution completed completed_episode_count = 300 episodes corresponding to 150 pairs; provider accounting shows model_calls_used = 150 because of shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generation per item, reused across conditions). Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm complete_pair_count = 150 and provider call counts (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl).

Detector outcomes and artifact‑documented persistence. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags in the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty of flagged rows. Because the detector persisted detailed fuzzy overlap outputs only when threshold events occurred (execution/transformation_manifest.json), the archive contains no global per‑item overlap table for post‑hoc inspection; this is an explicit, archived implementation behavior rather than a missing log.

Validator outcomes and primary statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The estimated paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numerical values and per‑episode validator traces are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/scoring/*.json).

Representative diagnostic. A representative episode (pair‑000001 / task‑000001) in execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json demonstrates the structure: normalized_response equals the normalized_reference_answer; parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 4; score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION); and the validator_trace includes initial/final state snapshots. This exemplar is included in the execution bundle and supports the numeric summaries above.
sections.discussion:
Reclassifying the prespecified primary test as degenerate. The reviewer correctly identified that the preregistered primary confirmatory estimand is rendered uninformative under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with a synthetic provenance sample: when one shared generation is reused across baseline and guarded episodes, and no high‑confidence exclusions occur, the pairwise comparison cannot observe generation‑level discordance. We therefore explicitly reclassify the primary test outcome reported above as a degenerate diagnostic: the observed n11 = 150 concordance documents a mechanical consequence of execution semantics and sample provenance rather than evidence that conservative detectors would find no contamination in independent web‑sourced benchmarks. This reclassification is supported by archived artifacts (execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv) and should guide appropriate interpretation.

Implementation lesson: detector persistence policy reduces interpretability. The detector implementation persisted full per‑item 5‑gram overlap outputs only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred (execution/transformation_manifest.json). While this reduced storage for the run, it prevents post‑hoc inspection of how close items were to the preregistered threshold. For future audits we recommend always persisting per‑item overlap scores (a new analysis/contamination_scores.csv) so sensitivity curves and near‑threshold cases can be inspected and adjudicated.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations for future, informative audits. To obtain non‑degenerate paired comparisons sensitive to web‑sourced contamination, the archive supports the following concrete changes that can be implemented within the same pipeline: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items (URLs/DOIs/timestamps) rather than synthetic items so provenance heuristics are meaningful; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded outputs are independently realized, increasing the chance of discordant pairs when contamination or memorization is stochastic or paraphrase‑sensitive; (3) persist full per‑item fuzzy overlap scores regardless of threshold crossings to enable sensitivity analysis; (4) expand to multi‑model replication and additional generation seeds to increase power and detect cross‑model leakage patterns; and (5) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from archived evidence (execution/model_configuration.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, analysis/contamination_summary.csv) and addresses the observed degeneracy mechanisms.

Operational caveats. Passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates the generated configurations satisfied the checked functional constraints for these synthetic tasks, but it does not imply production readiness or absence of semantic regressions beyond the validator's scope. Likewise, the absence of high‑confidence flags in this synthetic, shared‑generation run cannot be generalized to public, web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, archived paired audit of conservative contamination detectors in a reproducible NetOps pipeline. The executed sample (150 pairs) produced zero high‑confidence flags and identical validator pass rates (n11 = 150), but this outcome is degenerate for the preregistered confirmatory estimand because the run used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/task_manifest.jsonl). We explicitly reclassify the primary confirmatory test as uninformative for detecting public‑benchmark contamination under the executed configuration, explain the precise artifact‑level mechanics that produced the degeneracy, document an implementation policy that suppressed global per‑item overlap persistence (execution/transformation_manifest.json), and provide concrete, artifact‑anchored recommendations to make future audits sensitive to realistic leakage. All key artifacts (execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv) are archived and cited above for verification; readers should treat the present numeric null as a pipeline diagnostic rather than evidence about contamination prevalence in web‑sourced datasets.

LLM used: gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (version 5.0). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Representative executed artifacts include execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, and analysis/contamination_summary.csv; the full execution bundle contains raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and the transformation manifest (execution/transformation_manifest.json). After the autonomy lock, the AI system autonomously performed literature search, gap selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer‑review simulation, and revision. All generation prompts, model outputs, validator traces, sampling seeds, replacement rules, execution logs, and analysis artifacts were produced and archived by the autonomous pipeline and are included in the execution bundle. No manual human editing of technical content, analyses, references, figures, tables, captions, or the Disclosure Statement occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development and rehearsal runs occurred (permitted) but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence for this final study unless re‑created under the locked pipeline. The execution followed preregistered missingness, retry, and exclusion policies; no deviations occurred except that the executed confirmatory sample used deterministic synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") rather than sampling the public OpenAlex datasets listed in the preregistration's benchmark_scope, and the model configuration set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics). These executed choices and their supporting artifacts are recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, and execution/execution_manifest.json.
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
